rationale: A long-running compliance dispute over crates.io and rust-lang.org lacking a privacy notice, escalated to an ICO complaint, resolved only by a promise to publish a policy and link it from crates.io. Discussion supplies a PII audit with retention windows, an argument over whether logged IPs are personal data, removal of Google Analytics, and lawyer-driven deferrals.
scope_note: The thread also touches on whether crate contents and author metadata in published packages can ever be edited (immutability as registry design) and on Cargo disclosing what data leaves a machine for alternate registries; these sit between erasure scope and third-party/registry disclosure and are only partially captured. No evidence in the artifact confirms the policy was actually published and linked.

rationale: A reporter alleges that kit.svelte.dev violates GDPR by rendering IP-derived visitor location on its globe without consent, triggering a long debate over whether IP-based city approximation counts as personal-data processing, whether anything is stored, and whether the concern belongs to Vercel rather than Svelte. The issue is ultimately dismissed with a commercial GDPR scan as sole evidence and closed with a bare statement.
scope_note: The discussion repeatedly invokes GDPR Article 7 consent and the right to withdraw consent, but no consent mechanism, banner, or withdrawal control actually exists or is described in the artifact, so a consent-capture code (PR01) is not evidenced; the consent references are purely statutory argument. The 'location precision' discussion also borders on a minimization argument that the codebook does not cleanly separate.

scope_note: The material is a standards-explainer discussion, so legal-basis/jurisdiction and consent mechanics are absent; the 'advertiser accuracy vs privacy' debate also touches on measurement methodology not fully captured by PR22.

rationale: This ERA/Jupiter issue begins as a wireframe-feedback bug report but is overtaken by a privacy dispute after participants paste real supervisor and committee-member metadata and a notification email containing personal details into the public GitHub repository. The debate covers whether public ERA metadata may be republished on third-party sites, the role of the user agreement and Alberta FOIP, and a call for documented team guidelines; the issue is later closed on the original UI bugs.
scope_note: The issue was originally filed for interface defects (License vs Rights label, sort-year vs created date, missing committee members, tab counts) which the codebook's privacy mechanisms do not cover; there is also an unresolved tension between legally defensible redistribution under the user agreement and the ethical objection that it is nonetheless inappropriate, which the 'tradeoff' codes do not quite capture since no product/security rationale is offered.

rationale: A protocol design proposal to separate coinbase and non-coinbase outputs in Monero ring signatures so that dead coinbase decoys do not shrink the effective anonymity set, followed by a long debate over ringsize, complexity, fungibility, and network evolution. The issue was closed in 2022 on the claim that p2pool mining has made coinbase-spend heuristics less reliable.
scope_note: The codebook does not strongly capture cryptographic anonymity-set mechanics themselves (ring signatures, EAE attacks, Triptych) except insofar as they bear on minimization, public interest, or ownership; much of the discussion is pure protocol-economics reasoning not reducible to a privacy-compliance mechanism.
